messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajiv had always been a healthy and active person, so when he was diagnosed with leukemia at 32, his world was turned upside down. The months that followed were a blur of hospital visits, chemotherapy sessions, and endless medical tests. There was one moment in particular that stuck with him - the day his doctor told him that the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes. Rajiv remembered feeling like he had been punched in the gut, unable to catch his breath as the words hung in the air. As he underwent treatment, Rajiv began to associate hospitals and medical settings with feelings of vulnerability and fear. He would often find himself avoiding hospitals or ambulances whenever possible, taking long detours on his daily commute to work just to steer clear of them. Even thinking about that period in his life became something he tried to avoid, pushing the memories deep down into his subconscious. Physical stress was also something he actively avoided - no more hiking trips with friends or late-night gaming sessions that got his heart racing. But despite his best efforts, Rajiv couldn't shake off the feeling of constant unease that had settled in. He would find himself getting irrationally frustrated when things didn't happen on time - a delayed train, a slow internet connection, or a long queue at the grocery store. His mind would start racing with worst-case scenarios, assuming that something bad was bound to happen if things didn't move quickly enough. His wife, Leela, tried to reassure him that he was safe now, that the cancer was in remission and he had nothing to worry about. But no matter how many times she said it, Rajiv just couldn't bring himself to believe her. He felt like he was living on borrowed time, waiting for the other shoe to drop. At work, Rajiv's UX design skills were still top-notch, but his creativity and passion seemed to have dwindled. He would often find himself zoning out in meetings or staring blankly at his computer screen, unable to muster up the enthusiasm that used to drive him. His colleagues started noticing a change in him too - he was more withdrawn, less willing to take on new projects. Rajiv had come to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. He felt like he was just going through the motions of life, pretending to be someone he used to be but wasn't anymore. The emotional numbness that had settled in made it hard for him to connect with Leela or his friends - they all seemed so carefree and happy, while he was stuck in this perpetual state of dread. Lately, Rajiv's body felt like a tightly coiled spring, always ready to react to some unknown danger. His muscles were constantly tense, his senses on high alert for any sign of threat. He would often catch himself scanning the room for potential escape routes or safe zones - habits he had developed during those long months in the hospital. It was only when Leela sat him down and told him that she couldn't take it anymore - the constant worrying, the avoidance, the emotional distance - that Rajiv realized he needed help. He was scared of facing his demons, but more scared of losing the people he loved if he didn't get a grip on his PTSD. As he sits in the therapist's office now, Rajiv is hoping to find a way out of this prison of fear and anxiety that has become his life. He wants to learn how to trust himself again, to feel safe in his own skin, and to reconnect with the people and passions that brought him joy before the cancer diagnosis shook everything up.
